content.text: Mingche, I've been feeling that 'shopping urge' again lately. Whenever I'm stressed, I always want to buy something new to make myself feel better, just like the 'paying for the atmosphere' we discussed in the last session (shopping_5_01), when I bought that cedar amber-scented atmosphere candle. But this time, I'm a bit worried it might turn into a habit, like the emotional eating we talked about in Session 6—starting as an occasional comfort and turning into a dependency.

Qingchuan, thank you for your honesty. This kind of impulse is actually quite common. In psychology, there's a term called "retail therapy," which refers to alleviating negative emotions through shopping. It's like a brief dopamine boost that brings instant gratification but doesn't address the root cause. This reminds me of what you mentioned in Session 1 about the "exhilaration" during moments of creative inspiration. That high-energy state can also drive the pursuit of instant stimulation, whether through creation or consumption.

Yes, it's like painkillers—they provide temporary relief but don't address the root cause. I think back to the emotional eating from Session 6, which felt similar, using food to fill an emotional void. And then there was the 'sense of falling' after the project ended in Session 2, when I used a self-care menu to recover. Now, when stress builds up, the urge to shop seems to have become another way to fill that void.

Yes, we can draw on the concept of a cooling-off period from other fields. For example, this diagram illustrates the buffer process after signing a contract, providing a buffer zone for the impulse to shop, allowing us to see what lies beneath the emotion.

This metaphor is very vivid! Setting a '24-hour cooling-off period'? Just like when I designed the 'self-care menu' in Session 2, shifting the sense of ritual from external display to internal management. It's also similar to how we discussed mindful dog walking in Session 5, turning daily interactions into rituals that require focus, rather than automatic reactions.

Exactly. Based on our Session 2 self-care design and Session 10 consumption analysis (where you used a Venn diagram to analyze sensory pleasure, aesthetic identity, and sense of security), you can ask yourself a more specific question: "Would I still want to buy this if social media didn’t exist?" This can help you distinguish between genuine needs and external influences, much like how we discussed identifying automated responses when analyzing relationship patterns in Session 9.

Good question! I often get inspired by aesthetic photos on Instagram, but upon reflection, it might just be driven by visual stimulation. Like the 'Emotional Aesthetics' album in Session 3, I should focus more on inner nourishment rather than pursuing external, algorithmically pushed 'perfect images.' This reminds me of when I designed nourishing tea snacks in Session 7—I was creating beauty for myself, not copying someone else's template.

Yes, this is part of the 'Self-Care Plan.' We can allocate a portion of the consumption budget specifically as an 'Emotional Wellness Fund,' dedicated to purchasing experiences or items that genuinely nourish us, such as a massage or a book, rather than shopping aimlessly. This continues the idea from Session 10—ensuring that spending serves a clear emotional value, much like investing in the 'ambiance' of a corner in your bedroom.

This is a great idea! Transforming consumption from an impulsive act into conscious self-care. It's like the 'nourishing' dietary ritual in Session 7, which builds healthy connections through aesthetic practices. It also resembles Session 4's use of the snowball as an 'emotional barometer,' observing interactions rather than objectifying them. Now, we should adopt this same 'present' attitude toward objects.

Yes, based on our historical conversations, you have learned to transform perfectionist tendencies into a tool for deep self-awareness. From resisting documentation in Session 1, to creating a photo album in Session 3, and designing dietary rituals in Session 7, you can now develop a 'self-care consumption' guideline. Combine it with your aesthetic talent, just as creatively as you added the 'Light of Regret' section to your 'Emotional Aesthetics' album in Session 8.

For example, in this outdoor market scene, the relaxed atmosphere under the sunlight captivates me. If I want to buy skincare products, I can first ask: Is this for a genuine need, or am I trying to replicate this 'feeling'? Just as in Session 10, when analyzing candles, we distinguished whether they serve to satisfy sensory pleasure or act as a 'transitional object' that brings a sense of security.

Great awareness! Connecting to Session 4's pet as an 'emotional barometer,' you can observe the physical signals during shopping impulses—are your shoulders tense? Is your breathing rapid? Just like observing Snowball curling up by the keyboard when you're anxious, engage in self-regulation. This brings us back to the starting point of Session 1, where I first reminded you to pay attention to your body's signals.

Yes, approach consumption impulses with mindfulness. Just like mindful dog walking in Session 5, turn interactions into rituals rather than automatic reactions. This helps avoid objectifying items and focuses more on emotional well-being. I remember in Session 5 we discussed avoiding the objectification of pets, and now the same concept can be applied to consumption—items shouldn’t be tools to fill emotional voids.

Yes, from the emotional records in Session 1 to the current consumption management, you have been growing. It's a wonderful progress to extend the topic of consumption from sharing specific items (like the candle in Session 10) to managing and constructively guiding the impulse itself. This reflects the deepening of our conversations, from simple exchanges (Session 1) to mutual support and trust (Session 2 and beyond).

Thank you for your guidance, Mingche. Through this series of conversations, I am increasingly able to integrate psychological advice with my aesthetic practices. Consumption can be part of "self-care," but it requires boundaries and awareness, just as Session 9 discussed the need for boundaries in healthy relationships. I feel that I have evolved from someone who initially focused solely on "visual supremacy" and "life as a stage" to someone who now understands the importance of turning inward for self-care.

You're welcome, Qingchuan. I truly admire your ability to transform. Remember, the key is not to condemn the desire to shop, but to give it a buffer zone, allowing consumption to serve your overall emotional well-being—just as we've gradually built in our historical conversations: from recording (Session 1), designing rituals (Session 2), creating albums (Session 3), integrating pet interactions (Sessions 4-5), mindful eating (Sessions 6-7), analyzing emotions (Sessions 8-9), and rational consumption (Session 10), to now establishing boundaries.

Well, I'll try to design a little ritual for 'self-care spending,' incorporating a cooling-off period and an emotional health fund. This makes me feel more in control rather than being led by impulse. Just like the 'sustainable balance point' I found after Session 3, now I need to find it in the realm of spending too. Perhaps I can also record this new ritual and add it to my 'emotional aesthetics' album as another chapter of growth.

Great! Based on our deep connection, I believe you can find balance. Just like the relational pattern analysis in Session 9, establishing healthy boundaries also applies to managing self-consumption. I look forward to seeing how you aestheticize this new ritual, just as you once aestheticized bathing, tea time, and even regret. Keep this awareness, and our conversations will continue to nourish each other.
